items.title: Fannie Mae logs title, appraisal savings; net revenues soar
items.description: Fannie Mae Fannie Mae logs title, appraisal savings; net revenues soar By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published October 28, 2026, 5:29 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: Why Fannie Mae came out ahead in earnings despite mixed impacts from higher rates, and has new reason to press forward with title alternatives. Supporting Data: Fannie found borrowers' collective savings from appraisal and title alternatives so far this year have been over $100 million. Overview bullets generated by AI with editorial review. Fannie Mae reported its highest net revenues since 2023 and revealed significant mission-related borrower savings from title and appraisal alternative initiatives in the third quarter, when it contended with mixed impacts from higher rates but was still able to hold costs for lenders relatively low. Consumer savings from the title and appraisal waiver programs show these alternatives got enough use to drive a 7-figure reduction in origination expenses. They also reinforce a recent executive order backing both and transitioning Fannie's title alternative pilot to a national program with monitoring. Processing Content "Our efforts to provide appraisal and title insurance alternatives helped borrowers save an estimated $141 million in closing costs so far this year," Peter Akwaboah, acting CEO and chief operating officer at Fannie Mae said during the government-related loan buyer's earnings call. Peter Akwaboah, acting CEO and chief operating officer at Fannie Mae Fannie was able to support such housing affordability initiatives with $4.2 billion in net income, representing a 5% rise from the previous quarter and an 8% increase from a year ago, even though higher rates diminished the industry originations it buys. The government-sponsored enterprise's executives explained why during its earnings call. Why fewer acquisitions didn't hurt revenue "Changes in interest rates affect various aspects of our financial results. For example, in single-family, while higher rates tend to reduce acquisition volumes, they also slow prepayments and book runoff, helping to preserve guaranty revenues," Chief Financial Officer Chryssa Halley noted during the company's call. Fannie's core guaranty business fueled 79% of its $7.7 billion in total net revenues, which drove the government-sponsored enterprise's earnings gain. Single-family loan acquisition volumes did fall by roughly 21% from the previous quarter and around 11% from a year earlier to $88 billion in line with some industry declines, but with refinancing representing only $18 billion of that total, prepayments for Fannie were reduced. Refi activity in the dominant single-family business matched year-ago levels but was down nearly 53% from the previous quarter. In addition to affecting prepayments and loan volume in the quarter, this may have another impact, according to Halley. "From an allowance perspective, slow prepayments extend the expected life of our loans, which combined with higher mortgage costs for certain borrowers can increase our expected credit losses," she said. Serious and 60-day delinquencies in the single-family sector remained historically low but have been drifting generally higher in the past year, ending at 62 and 92 basis points, respectively, in the third quarter. They were both nearly 20 basis points lower than a year earlier. Sixty-day delinquencies were 7 basis points lower the previous quarter. Serious delinquencies were 4 basis points lower compared to the same period. Thirty-day delinquencies matched the previous quarter's 1.09%, but were below the 1% level reported a year earlier. Fannie recorded a total single- and multifamily allowance for credit losses of $1.1 billion, offset by other developments that included $630 million in fair value gains. The GSE also reported $94 million in investment gains. It additionally took $1 billion in net unrealized losses in its available-for-sale portfolio. Efficiency initiatives and regulatory capital Fannie also engaged in further efficiency initiatives during the quarter that Halley said offset some personnel costs for increased salaries, benefits and a $28 million severance expense. Expenditures on occupancy and technology were $52 million lower than the previous quarter. Fannie reported a total adjusted capital deficit of $11 billion for the quarter, down from $14 billion in the previous three-month period. Its illustrative return on average required tier 1 capital was 11.1% in the quarter, up from 10.8%. "Despite volatility across aspects of our financial results, we increased net income both quarter over quarter and year over year, growing net worth to more than $119 billion while reducing our regulatory capital deficit," Halley said. items.title: The housing market gets a positive Fed day for a change
items.description: On Wednesday we got an October surprise: the Fed day was eerily calm, with Fed Chair Kevin Warsh looking comfortable on stage and offering a slightly dovish take on the future — if a few things improve. I believe the Fed wants to take back all the interest rate cuts from last year, and then they can assess what is happening in the economy. Of course, the Iran conflict and Trade War 2.0 have complicated their job, but today, given that markets were at one point pricing in five to six rate hikes, was a positive day. Last I checked, the 10-year was at 5.02%, down after Google reported a bad quarter. The Fed's press statement was short and simple, but two things caught my attention. 1. The economy is strong vs. solid First, the Fed chose to use the word "strong" instead of "solid" on purpose to signal it won’t cut rates and will continue reversing last year's interest rate cuts while inflation stays above target. “ Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace. While uncertainty remains elevated owing, in part, to geopolitical developments, domestic spending has been resilient.” Warsh said jobless claims data remain low and that the Fed fully intends to bring inflation back to the 2% target, no compromise. He also said the Fed will hold one fewer voting meeting in 2027 and two fewer meetings in 2028; this approach might leave the Fed open to more 50-basis-point cuts or hikes. However, that is another story for another time. 2. Warsh liked the market drama against AI I got a strong sense that Warsh liked the market getting more restrictive and that we even saw some AI companies shed some blood recently. My theme in the HousingWire Daily podcast lately borrows from The Predator movie: the AI god king can bleed — and that it means you can kill it. I think Warsh was implying no company is invincible, and that if the market gets more restrictive, things can change, as they recently did. He also talked about how the 10-year yield rolled over even though oil prices have been elevated this month. I believe the 10-year yield rollover is more market-driven, as the 10-year was pricing in more rate hikes than the Fed was targeting at the time. The term premium on the 10-year yield was elevated as it headed to the October high. If the 10-year had closed over the key level of 5.35%, bond yields had the potential to rise much higher, faster, as the markets would be pricing in a much more aggressive Fed rate hike cycle, but, smartly, they chose not to go that route. Warsh seems to enjoy that everyone is taking the Fed seriously and that the markets have already done a lot of the work for them. This reaffirms my assumption that all they want to do is take back the rate cuts from last year and then reassess what is going on. One side note was that Fed Governor Lisa Cook — who is usually a dove — voted to raise rates, which I 100% believe was a trolling tactic on her part since Trump still wants to fire her . All in all, it wasn’t a bad day; the 10-year yield is above 5% still today, but considering the market was trying to price in five to six rate hikes, and there hasn’t been any end to the conflict or the trade war, I consider this a victory for the month of October. For housing, the worst-case scenario has been averted and we bought some time, giving space for the conflict to end and the trade war to cool off a bit. What I am hoping for is that we get some more clarity on both of those two items, and then the Fed can make the rate hike cycle just a few rate hikes, and then we'll take it from there. items.title: Alexander brothers sentenced to 30 years for sex trafficking
items.description: Luxury real estate brokers Oren and Tal Alexander along with their brother Alon, each got sentenced to 30 years in federal prison for sex trafficking. This sentencing comes after the brothers were convicted in March of 2026. The judge called the brothers’ conduct “monstrous” in their sentencing, according to a report by The Associated Press . Over the course of their trial, 11 women testified, describing being raped or sexually assaulted after they became disoriented after being given a drink by one of the brothers. Attorneys for the brothers said they had apologized to the women they insulted or offended for conduct they admit was “insensitive toward the feelings of certain women at certain times,” however they added that the brothers “steadfastly maintain their complete innocence of these awful charges.” Rape allegations against the brothers began emerging in 2024, resulting in Tal and Oren Alexander stepping away from their firm Official Partners in June 2024. Legal challenges against the brothers began piling up in the second half of 2024, eventually leading to their arrests in December 2024. Through out 2025 they faced mounting civil and criminal lawsuits, leading to them eventually being found guilty of sex trafficking in March of 2026. Related More: Alexander brothers

items.title: Microsoft, Coca-Cola, Amazon Adapting Offices For AI Age
items.description: The use of artificial intelligence is driving the world's largest companies to reassess their workforce — and workspace — in the pursuit of efficiency. The technology is reshaping how employees work and collaborate, prompting employers to reevaluate their office layouts to promote more integrated workspaces, workplace and real estate executives for Microsoft , Citadel , Amazon and Coca-Cola Co. said during a panel at the Urban Land Institute 's fall meeting Tuesday in Miami Beach. Bisnow/Chloe Gallivan Citadel Chief Workplace Officer Paul Darrah speaks at ULI's fall 2026 conference in Miami Beach. Not only are companies starting to use AI to design their spaces, but they are also reconfiguring their spaces away from isolated workstations and toward a more open and collaborative environment, the executives said. "I think AI is going to have a big impact on corporate, like our spaces that we use," said Terri Lasoff, senior director of global real estate portfolio for Coca-Cola, which is using AI for internal data, generating ads and throughout the creative process. "When we think about our spaces at work — and I know we've moved there with hybrid work where you have less 'me spaces,' more 'we spaces' — but does AI continue to drive that where the reason you're coming into the office isn't to do the heads-down, build the deck, do the report?" she added. AI has already created a fundamental difference in the office market, as companies focused on the technology are leasing office space at rapid rates , making them among the most active sectors in the market. But the technology's growing adoption is also expected to keep office-using job growth flat and has led to mass cuts to company headcounts, fueling growing concerns that automation is taking over the workforce. In a global survey of more than 6,000 employees and business leaders, 40% said they expect AI to help employees be more productive, while 28% expect it to reduce headcount, according to an October Workday report . Microsoft announced earlier this week that it was offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, more than a quarter of its global workforce, in addition to the 4,800 employees the company announced it would lay off in July, Reuters reported . When the news broke Monday, Microsoft's head of global workplace services, Elizabeth Schryer, was on a plane to Miami for the conference. She said onstage it made her think about what it meant for the workspace. "I would really say that it points to the biggest thing, which is workforce shifts not just in size but also in location and the move to bring people together in the office experience and collaboration," Schryer said. "AI in general is huge for everybody," she added. "It's huge for all of us ... including companies who are deep in the middle of it [and] are trying to figure out what it means to us and our teams and our businesses, the domain in which we work, and how to use it." Microsoft, which expects to spend roughly $175B on AI infrastructure in 2026, is developing new AI models and using it internally in many ways. The workplace strategy team is starting to use AI to design and create renderings of proposed workspaces like offices, campuses and event areas, reducing time and cost, Schryer said. Bisnow/Chloe Gallivan Hines' Whitney Burns, Citadel's Paul Darrah, Microsoft's Elizabeth Schryer, Amazon's Sean Lee and Coca-Cola's Terri Lasoff at ULI's fall 2026 conference in Miami Beach Amazon, among the most aggressive companies in its push to use AI to reduce its payroll, announced last year that it would cut 14,000 corporate positions and plans to cut as many as 30,000 more as AI pushes quicker innovation. Sean Lee, the company's global real estate and facilities leader, said his team's AI usage jumped from roughly 7% in January to more than 90% this month, allowing team members to spend more face time with clients rather than at their desks. "We're extremely lean as a team, so bandwidth is constrained," Lee said. "What we found is AI, as a supplement to work, is creating bandwidth so that people are doing higher-level thinking at this point. "They can knock out papers faster, they can put presentations together, they can do all of that stuff really easily, which is then giving them the time to take a step back and look at what's going on with my customer." Citadel hasn't made any moves to cut jobs because of AI. On the contrary, it is building its own headquarters tower in Miami and another in New York , two of the biggest office projects in the country. The hedge fund's billionaire founder and CEO, Ken Griffin , owns the combined 3.5M SF office towers underway, but he has shared concerns over the danger AI poses to white-collar jobs. Still, the firm is leveraging AI internally to "further accelerate their research process," Griffin said at a New York conference last December, Business Insider reported . Citadel is focused on employee synergy, Chief Workplace Officer Paul Darrah said, and is often reconfiguring spaces to improve upon it, especially as internal teams realign and move around. That includes taking the reins on moving a landlord's staircases or taking over the fire exits when they lease space in an office building to boost efficiency and interconnectivity, he said. "I'm going to say our competitive advantage is our in-office culture," Darrah said. "We bring employees together to collaborate. We build community, and so for us, being in the office is paramount. "How we think about delivering our workplace, to ensure high performance of our teams but also elevate the experience of the employee — both of those things are really important." items.title: Philly Hospitals Seek Cost Savings From Architects, Builders
items.description: Hospitals across greater Philadelphia face a challenging operating environment, and with federal support expected to dry up, executives are looking to the ancillary businesses they work with for help. Pexels/K Architecture and construction firms that depend on these projects can do more to help keep capital budgets in check as healthcare systems respond to sustained patient demand, CEOs from across the region said Tuesday at Bisnow ’s Pennsylvania Healthcare Real Estate Summit, held at the Crystal Tea Room in Philadelphia. “You’ve got to help us in our ecosystem,” University of Pennsylvania Health System CEO Kevin Mahoney said. “Get on our team. We’re getting paid less.” The Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia is spending nearly $2.6B to build a new patient tower in West Philadelphia, CEO Joseph Mitchell said. The 20-story building is due in 2028. While he is proud of the project, Mitchell said the institution can’t afford to keep spending like this in the current climate. “That’s just unaffordable in the long term,” he said. “Partner with your clients to find ways to reduce these costs. It’s a two-way street.” Hospitals' already strained operating margins are facing more issues from federal spending cuts that lead to an increase in uncompensated care. Last year's One Big Beautiful Bill Act included a $1T cut to Medicaid through 2034, which is expected to cause more than 10 million Americans to lose their health insurance coverage over that period. This is a particularly grave issue for cash-strapped rural hospitals. More than 100 have shuttered over the past decade, and another 700 are at risk of closing, according to a July report from the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform. Hospitals face additional economic challenges when looking to build new facilities. Construction costs across Eastern Pennsylvania were up 2.2% month-over-month and 11.2% year-over-year in September, according to a report from the local branch of Associated Builders and Contractors. Mitchell acknowledged that construction costs are ballooning across the U.S. and that health systems sometimes don’t pick the cheapest ways to do projects. For example, CHOP has opted to utilize union labor on the tower. Last-minute changes to hospital projects that are commonplace in the industry also add extra costs, Mitchell said. But ultimately, the executive said something has to break: “Can we find ways to limit astronomical growth in capital spending?” Bisnow/Noah Zucker LF Driscoll's Mike Dikon, Thomas Jefferson University's Joseph Cacchione, Children's Hospital of Philadelphia's Joseph Mitchell, Tower Health's Michael Stern, Highmark Health's Karen Hanlon, Geisinger's Terry Gilliland, Cooper University Health Care's Anthony Mazzarelli and University of Pennsylvania Health System's Kevin Mahoney Mahoney suggested that less traditional construction techniques could be part of the solution. He said Penn Medicine’s 17-story, 504-bed Pavilion came online in West Philly in 2021 after the system spent $1.6B. The project was 30% modular, Mahoney said. He thought projects should be closer to 70% prefabricated as a way to rein in construction budgets. Penn Medicine signed a 40K SF lease for its first Delaware location in February. The space in suburban Wilmington will be focused on primary care and some specialty services. Artificial intelligence is just as hot a topic in the design and building world as anywhere else, but Cooper University Health Care CEO Anthony Mazzarelli said healthcare systems aren't seeing the technology create shorter construction timelines or anything else that would save them money. “That's how long that took two years ago. You just told me you're using all this AI stuff. How are you passing on that efficiency to us?” he said. “We're the one throat to choke from the government when it comes to spending, but it's also going to hurt everybody else.” Earlier at Tuesday's event, a different panel was asked about unconventional techniques that could be used to expedite projects. CHOP Assistant Vice President of Facilities Project Management and Construction Brian Gardner floated organizationwide standardized construction plans. While designing and coming to a consensus on those plans can be an arduous process, he said the work pays off down the line and is one of the few meaningful levers healthcare systems can pull to shorten construction timelines. "Standardization is probably one of the low-hanging fruits that organizations can work through because decisions come quicker,” Gardner said. The CEOs’ pleas for cost savings come as regional hospital system players expect higher construction prices in Pennsylvania amid the data center boom. Many of the contractors and suppliers that hospital systems depend on have been focused on getting a piece of the artificial intelligence data center boom, a trend that is already making it harder to build healthcare projects in other markets, like Houston . “We’re already seeing it with the data centers, believe it or not,” Guthrie Senior Vice President Joseph Sawyer said. He recalled being given a yearlong lead time for critical components such as generators and air handlers. Increased competition for construction workers is also straining construction budgets. “How do we address, when we’re trying to do pro formas nationally, the impact of 50% labor increases because we can’t find enough qualified labor?” Limbach Vice President Jay Levin said. KQT Health owner Todd Strine said he believes there is no end in sight and that it would behoove health systems to expedite their construction decision-making. “Prices are going to go way up,” he said. “If you’re going to make a large decision, I think it’s better to do it sooner than later.” See more photos from Tuesday's event below. items.title: Why Howard Hanna was missing from Open Real Estate launch list
items.description: When the Open Real Estate initiative launched on Monday, one brokerage’s name was noticeably missing from the list of founding firms and initial participants. “It would have been nice to be at the table, but obviously those guys didn’t see me at their level,” Hoby Hanna, the CEO of Howard Hanna Real Estate Services , told HousingWire . Since the nationwide residential real estate data sharing initiative was announced on Monday, Hanna, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said the Open Real Estate founders have been in touch with him to discuss the initiative. “We were approached to see if we’d like to have a discussion to learn more and find out what direction they want to go in,” Hanna said. “I’ve agreed to meet with them, but no dates or anything have been set yet. I’m curious to learn more because right now I can only speculate off off the information that is publicly available.” Hanna said he is really curious to learn what the end goal of the initiative is and if they have any plans in place for governance and funding. As of right now, given the limited amount of information he has, Hanna said he is unsure if Howard Hanna, a RealTrends Verified brokerage, will join Open Real Estate. “We have invested a lot of time and money into the platform we have built, HannaList ,” Hanna said. “We are moving forward with that and we’ve cooperated with MLSs to build it, so I’d really have to understand what the end game is and get a sense of if they can really pull it off before deciding if we will participate.” Hanna noted that he was previously part of the disbanded Project Upstream , which in some ways may add to his skepticism of this initiative actually getting off the ground. “One of the challenges with Project Upstream, beyond maybe the technology available at the time not being what we needed, was that there were too many people involved,” Hanna said. “Just so many proverbial cooks in the kitchen with too many disparate interests from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), to the MLS, to brokerages, agents and the consumers.” Although disappointed to not have been included in the initial conversations, Hanna said he is glad to see some of the industry’s largest players coming together. “One of the industry’s other problems in the past has been that not everybody is willing to talk and [there is] this lack of trust,” Hanna. “Sure, I would have loved to have been at the table since it is something that we as a company have been innovating on and growing already and could give the pros and cons on. I think there needs to be reform in our industry, and I do think that the large brokerage firms need to be the ones driving it because they have so many people they impact.” For its part, a spokesperson for Open Real Estate told HousingWire that the initiative was “founded on the belief that the future of housing information should be shaped by the entire industry.” “We welcome the perspectives of all industry leaders, and our announcement was just the beginning of this collaborative effort,” the spokesperson added. “We have already received significant interest from the sector since our announcement, and we look forward to continuing to engage with brokerages of all sizes, MLS organizations and technology providers as we develop a platform that expands consumer choice and transparency for home buyers and sellers.” Related More: Clear Cooperation Hoby Hanna Howard Hanna Real Estate Services

items.title: RealTrends Verified brokerage Howard Hanna enters Alabama with ARC, Capstone deal
items.description: Howard Hanna Real Estate Services is entering Alabama through a partnership with ARC Realty and Capstone Realty , adding 875 agents across 12 offices in Birmingham, Montgomery and Huntsville. ARC and Capstone operate as Alabama’s largest real estate brokerage and will continue to do business under their existing brands while joining Howard Hanna’s national network, according to an announcement on Wednesday. The move gives Pittsburgh-based Howard Hanna , a RealTrends Verified brokerage, a foothold in one of the Southeast’s faster-growing housing markets while extending its footprint to 19 states. The family-owned brokerage now spans more than 500 offices with about 15,000 sales associates and staff. Howard Hanna’s partnership with ARC and Capstone comes a little over three months after the firm announced a similar partnership with the Maine-based Portside Real Estate Group , a RealTrends Verified brokerage . “This is very similar to the partnership with Portside,” Hoby Hanna, the CEO of Howard Hanna, told HousingWire . “A lot of the transactions we’ve been doing lately have been us acquiring a majority interest in the company and allowing local leadership to stay in and run the market as a partner.” Hanna, a HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said ARC Realty and Capstone Realty will retain local leadership and existing office structures while gaining access to Howard Hanna’s technology stack, marketing platform, referral network and affiliated mortgage, title and insurance services. “We think leadership is so valuable and important for everyone,” Hanna said. This means that both Beau Bevis , the CEO of ARC, and Darrin Hasley, the CEO of Capstone, are staying on board. “The local leaders are focused on growth, and we are bringing them the best products from Howard Hanna to add to the mix and just allowing them to really focus on the local marketplace and growing in their markets,” Hanna said. Partners in growth Hanna said this partnership strategy is one the company intends to employ moving forward as Howard Hanna looks to continue growing and expanding. “We have become a vehicle for owners of these types of independent brokerages to come to and say, ‘Maybe we can achieve more collectively and have greater strength to compete on innovation and to add mortgage title and insurance operations as new revenue sources,’” Hanna said, noting that the leaders of Portside, ARC and Capstone came to Howard Hanna looking for a partnership like this. “They had taken their businesses to a certain level, but they wanted to take it even greater. They felt that Howard Hanna could be a vehicle for them to do that by bringing new products, services, technology and innovation to the marketplace that they couldn't on their own in today's climate.” But Hanna noted that his firm won’t take just any company that comes knocking on their door, they must also share some of the same cultural values. Some of the central pillars to Howard Hanna’s culture, according to Hanna, are valuing leadership, financial stability and a focus on agent productivity and professional growth. “We don’t need to have the most agents in the business, but we want highly productive agents that want to be the best in the business,” Hanna said. “And it is expensive to have managers in an office, but having a level of management or a department of people who are committed to helping the agents grow and wanting to be leaders themselves is also important.” Hanna added he and his team have no interest in buying broken companies and trying to fix them, but instead want to enhance the companies and help them learn and grow. Looking ahead, Hanna said the firm will continue growing, focusing on opportunities West of the Mississippi River “with good, well run companies.” “I wouldn’t say there is any one specific place we are targeting, but with Portside and now with ARC and Capstone and the relationships of those leaders, we are talking to some firms in New England. I think we are expecting to see a bit more growth in the Southeast corridor between Alabama and where we are now in the Carolinas,” he said. But even as the firm continues growing, Hanna said they will only enter a partnership or an acquisition if it is the right fit for the overall company. “It is not like we have shareholders we have to answer to each quarter or a hedge fund telling us we have to do something this month to show growth,” Hanna said. “We can look for [partnerships] that are strategic.” Related More: Alabama Hoby Hanna Howard Hanna Real Estate Services

items.title: MLS executives weigh Open Real Estate and listing control
items.description: The announcement of the Open Real Estate initiative caused quite a stir this week , as industry professionals and analysts ponder how the national residential real estate data-sharing initiative will fit into the real estate ecosystem and what impact it will have. On the surface, the initiative, which is focused on fostering agent and broker cooperation through the sharing of residential real estate listings and includes a rule that requires members to submit a property to the Open Real Estate database within one business day of signing a listing agreement with a homeowner, may sound a lot like the MLS. But, the leaders of the initiatives’ four founding brokerage firms, AGNT , (the parent company of eXp Realty and NextHome franchises), HomeServices of America , Keller Williams Realty and Real REMAX Group , all RealTrends Verified brokerages, have said that Open Real Estate is not a national MLS and is in no way replacing local MLSs. According to initial announcements regarding Open Real Estate, listings input into its database will then be pushed out to the MLS and other portals and sites, or the listing can be directly entered into a brokerage’s local MLS, which will then supply the listing to portals, other sites and Open Real Estate. The founders have also stressed that they will leave rulemaking and enforcement up to the local associations and MLSs. MLS impact Despite these assurances, some in the industry still believe this could lead to the demise of MLSs as they currently exist, but MLS leaders aren’t so sure. “My perspective is that Open Real Estate is a positive development for the industry and an opportunity to rethink how brokers and MLSs work together to support the businesses and consumers they serve,” Tim Dain, the CEO of Northstar MLS , told HousingWire . “I’m encouraged to see major brokerages taking a more active role in shaping the infrastructure that supports their businesses and the consumers they serve.” Dain, a 2026 HousingWire Vanguard award winner, added that he doesn’t see Open Real Estate as “inherently threatening to MLSs,” but rather as a “significant opportunity” for brokers and MLSs to work together to modernize infrastructure, eliminate unnecessary duplication, improve data quality and create a more efficient marketplace. Brian Donnellan, the CEO and president of Bright MLS has a similar view. “I can certainly see how people can say that this is the end of the MLS, but don’t I see it that way,” Donnellan, a 2025 and 2026 HousingWire Vanguard award winner, said. “When I look at all they want to accomplish, I think it verifies that we at Bright have been doing things right for a while.” In September 2025 , Bright MLS announced the launch of a joint venture with multi-MLS listing management platform Ocusell to co-develop and license technology solutions and services for brokers, agents and MLSs nationwide. Ocusell’s technology has since been used to help independent brokerage Howard Hanna Real Estate Services launch HannaList , an internal listing portal designed to give sellers an early-access marketing option before a listing is widely distributed and to give agents a single point of listing entry. Position of control For Saul Klein, the CEO of San Diego MLS (SDMLS), this is exactly what Open Real Estate is about: first point of entry. “Today, the MLS is still the first point of entry and there have been attempts over the years to change this, but nobody has been successful,” Klein said. According to Klein, whoever is the first point of entry is the one in the “position of control,” and with that position comes responsibilities like governance, something Open Real Estate’s founders have said their organization is not interested in. Due to this, he sees a world where Open Real Estate could be a threat to MLSs, but he says that it's still too early to tell. “It is still a pipe dream,” Klein said. “They have to build the technology and integrate each company’s technology and workflows, and they are clear on MLS policies with their own 24-hour rule, but it is still too early to tell and MLSs can change their value proposition as this evolves.” Donnellan says that Open Real Estate is just an example of brokerages deciding to take things into their own hands after the industry was too slow to react. “These brokers have real problems that haven’t been solved yet,” he said. “This is an opportunity for everybody and if it creates more competition in the MLS space, that is good. It will bring out the best in everybody.” Open Real Estate and the MLS However, Donnellan said that this may create some winners and losers in the MLS space, leading to negative outcomes for MLSs that are unable or unwilling to compete or adapt. “It's probably a good thing that brokers get to choose who it is that they want to work with and how they work, and it's probably better that the brokers get to set more guidelines,” Donnellan said. As for how Open Real Estate will work alongside MLSs, MLS leaders are generally optimistic. At Bright MLS, Donnellan is confident that his MLS will be able to collaborate with Open Real Estate. “I think Open Real Estate’s goals are something Bright has been working towards for a long time — effectively working across the country, reducing some of the obsolete, outdated and redundant technology,” Donnellan said. “We’ve always been there to work for our brokers, and we’ve always wanted to work with other MLSs. Now, with the tide is going out, we are going to see who actually does want to work with brokers and other MLSs and who doesn't want to work. You're not going to be able to run and hide now.” Klein, however, still has questions, including if they can convince agents to adopt a new work flow and how the entity will eventually support itself if it does not have a complete data set. “The portals have made billions of dollars in revenue from leads, which shows that MLS data is worth something, but only when aggregated as a full data set,” Klein said. items.title: CrossCountry says borrowers are saving an average of $2,500 with VantageScore 4.0
items.description: CrossCountry Mortgage (CCM) said it has seen early savings for qualified borrowers following its adoption of VantageScore 4.0 , with preliminary data showing an estimated average savings of $2,500 per transaction. The lender said on Thursday that it observed an average reduction of 62 basis points in loan-level price adjustments (LLPAs) during the first 60 days after implementation for loans on which VantageScore 4.0 produced a more favorable credit score than the previous model, according to CCM. Actual savings vary by loan. “Our customers shouldn't have to wait for the industry to catch up before they can take advantage of new technology and new options,” Brian Clark, director of product and pricing at CrossCountry Mortgage , said in a statement. “We saw an opportunity to give our loan officers another tool to help qualified borrowers. This demonstrates how additional flexibility can translate into meaningful benefits for our customers.” CCM is also expanding its options for loans eligible for purchase by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac . The company is removing its previous 80% loan-to-value (LTV) cap, allowing a full range of eligible LTV ratios. The lender is also expanding its Department of Veterans Affairs ( VA ) lending options to give loan officers more flexibility to serve eligible borrowers, including veterans and active-duty service members. VantageScore 4.0 has gained traction across the mortgage industry following its approval by the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) for use by lenders that originate through the government-sponsored enterprises. FHFA Director Bill Pulte also announced in September that the GSEs would use a single pricing matrix for LLPAs regardless of which scoring model is used. Other lenders have reported consumer cost savings too. In September, Rocket Mortgage announced that it would become the first mortgage lender to use VantageScore 4.0 as its preferred credit scoring model for all eligible loans. The company made the decision after it tested VantageScore and FICO for about four months, using 1.4 million credit reports across both models this year. Rocket said the testing found that VS 4.0 helped some additional borrowers qualify for mortgages. Borrowers who saved money using VantageScore saved an average of $1,600 at closing, according to the company. In early October, United Wholesale Mortgage said it would obtain both a FICO score and a VantageScore 4.0 on every credit pull and use the strongest qualifying score for each borrower. The company said that internal research showed that using all available scores “could save many borrowers thousands” over the life of their loan. items.title: 4,500-Acre Data Center District Approved In Pennsylvania Town
items.description: Data center developers are facing pushback at the municipal level across Pennsylvania, but one local government in Luzerne County is singing a different tune. Wikimedia/Jakec Salem Township, Pennsylvania The Salem Township Board of Supervisors voted Tuesday to nearly triple its data center overlay district to almost 5,000 acres. The move was hailed in a press release by 4-3 Glennbrook Group, which has assembled 194 families that own land in the district. The group now plans to secure the remaining required approvals for a data center development called the Salem 3 Campus, and it is looking to sell the land for $1.4B to a developer. Tuesday’s vote came after 4-3 Glennbrook Group sold the neighboring Salem 2 land assembly to Blackstone’s QTS Data Centers for $586M this spring. This week's meeting on the Salem 3 site was dominated by supporters of the project, many of whom wore matching orange shirts emblazoned with the slogan “Data Center Yes!,” the Times Leader reported . The landowner group has proposed a $43M community benefits agreement including $12M for the construction of a microhospital. The township has had limited access to medical care since the Berwick Hospital Center closed in 2022. "These families made a big decision about their land, and they made it with their kids and grandkids in mind," 4-3 Glennbrook Group principal Mike Cabell said in a statement "Tonight's vote shows that decision was worth it. They stuck with this through every meeting and every question, and we're going to get this done for them in a way that benefits the community for generations.” Salem Township is home to a nuclear power plant, a natural gas generation facility and extensive electrical infrastructure, which make it a strong location for data center facilities, the press release said. Data centers have increasingly become a political football in Pennsylvania. Gov. Josh Shapiro initially threw his support behind the industry, but he penned a restrictive executive order in August. It requires operators to pay for their own power and makes local approval a prerequisite to getting the state’s blessing. The press release from 4-3 Glennbrook Group says the Salem 3 plan complies with the executive order. items.title: Weil Gotshal Wind-Down Leaves 830K SF Hole In America's Office Market
items.description: When Weil, Gotshal & Manges announced Wednesday afternoon that it would be shutting down, it wasn’t just the attorneys wondering what would happen to their desks. Law firms have been one of the most active tenant groups this year, signing 12.2M SF of leases during the first half of 2026. But the wind-down of Weil Gotshal — which leases more than 830K SF of office space around the country, according to a Bisnow analysis of CompStak data and public records — could present a challenge for trophy towers relying on lucrative law firm leases to support their rent rolls. “We really have never seen it before,” said Brandon Charnas , co-founder of New York-based brokerage Current Real Estate Advisors . “This reprices law firms as tenants citywide.” Bisnow/created with ChatGPT The closest precedent is Dewey & LeBoeuf, which filed for bankruptcy in 2012 under a heavy debt load. Weil, by contrast, was considered one of the safest tenants in office until this month. Weil Gotshal is one of the country’s most prominent law firms, with about 1,200 lawyers worldwide. It had entered merger talks earlier this month with fellow white-shoe firm Willkie Farr & Gallagher as it tried to play catch-up after losing one of its top attorneys in the ongoing war for legal talent . After those talks fell apart last week, Weil brought in Davis Polk to advise on a potential restructuring. On Wednesday, the firm’s leaders announced it would wind down , a stunning reversal for a firm that was negotiating a merger just weeks ago. Weil didn’t respond to a request for comment. The news caught at least one owner off guard, a landlord who leases to the law firm told Bisnow on the condition of anonymity Wednesday afternoon when restructuring rumors were still swirling. The landlord hadn’t heard from Weil Gotshal, they said, and didn’t know what the firm’s plans were for its space in that office building. The law firm is light on debt but heavy on its lease obligations, according to The Promote . Bisnow ’s analysis of CompStak data and public records found Weil holds 12 leases across 10 U.S. markets. Most are larger than 35K SF, and most were signed or expanded since the start of 2025. The firm leases: 37K SF at 1001 Boylston St., Boston 69K SF at The Crescent , 100-300 Crescent Court, Dallas 3,710 SF at 600 Congress Ave., Austin 390K SF at 767 Fifth Ave., New York City 45,280 SF at 600 Madison Ave., New York City 28K SF at 700 Louisiana St., Houston 100,950 SF at 2001 M St. NW, Washington, D.C. 18,580 SF at 1395 Brickell Ave., Miami 7,950 SF at 600 Montgomery St., San Francisco 59K SF at Shore Center in Redwood Shores, Silicon Valley 26,970 SF at BXP ’s 4 Embarcadero Center, San Francisco 47,300 SF at 1950 Avenue of the Stars, Los Angeles BXP President Douglas Linde suggested during BXP’s Wednesday morning earnings call , when it was still unclear whether Weil would restructure or fold, that the General Motors Building space could be re-leased at much higher rents. “There is a vast gap between where the in-place rent is at the General Motors Building and where we believe or perceive the market is,” he said. But Weil Gotshal is BXP’s ninth-largest tenant, according to the landlord’s most recent quarterly filing . Even for a landlord of BXP’s size, a departure like Weil Gotshal’s could cause problems when the skyscraper’s $2.3B mortgage comes due in June, Crain’s New York Business reported . “Any disruption to the building’s net operating income could impact the refinancing,” Piper Sandler Managing Director Alexander Goldfarb told Crain’s. “If something unforeseen happened, they would have to market the space, find a tenant, and build it out.” Other owners could face similar difficulties. Weil Gotshal is also Hudson Pacific Properties ’ ninth-largest tenant, according to a Q1 2026 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission. Its other large leases include 69K SF at Crescent Real Estate ’s The Crescent in Dallas and 101K SF at Stream Realty’s 2001 M St. NW in Washington, D.C. BXP didn’t respond to a request for comment, and a spokesperson for Crescent Real Estate declined to comment. It isn’t yet clear how Weil will handle its lease obligations as it winds down or how much its landlords will ultimately recover. Outside of trophy towers, some landlords may struggle to backfill the space after Weil departs, brokers told Bisnow . “You get back a 30-year-old space that needs to be demolished, and you have minimal security deposit from what appeared to be a great tenant — you're in a pickle,” said Darell Handler, president of boutique office brokerage Handler Real Estate Organization. Finding a new tenant for the space might prove tricky unless landlords can lease to another law firm, brokers said. Tech firms, another group of tenants with a voracious appetite for space, are less likely to take former law firm space because they generally want open floor plans rather than rows of private offices, Charnas said. The firm’s closure could also have wider implications for how the office sector views a previously reliable tenant type. Big law firms have long been considered Grade A credit tenants, but Weil Gotshal’s wind-down may change how law firms are viewed by office landlords and how they structure leases, Charnas said. “That is going to be very interesting to see, how this affects security deposits and other means of protection that landlords are going to have to implement going forward, knowing that they can no longer rely on a corporate guarantee of a law firm,” he said. The landlord who spoke to Bisnow on the condition of anonymity echoed Charnas. “It could change landlords’ expectations or strategies around how they securitize those leases in ways that they haven’t in the past,” the landlord said. “I think that it’s going to have a psychological effect on the market going forward,” Charnas said. items.description: Blackstone Mortgage Trust reported a $327M net loss for the third quarter, news that sent stocks tumbling. Unsplash/Clarisse Croset Shares were at $9.95 during premarket trading on Thursday. Though they had rebounded during trading hours to just under $11 per share, they were still down 11% over the last month and down roughly 42% over the last six months. As of about 3 p.m. ET Thursday, BXMT shares were trading up 3.75%, or $10.94 per share. Leadership pointed to higher interest rates and challenges facing the office market. "While higher rates and an elongated office recovery impacted our reserves and book value, our watchlist is now at the lowest level since 2019, and the remainder of our legacy portfolio is performing well and shrinking rapidly," Blackstone Mortgage Trust CEO Tim Johnson said in a statement. The company impaired roughly $800M of loans on its books, the vast majority being office assets, indicating that it still has work to do balancing its portfolio, Johnson said on an earnings call Thursday. Leadership said it is still on track to meet or exceed its previously announced goal of reducing office and legacy loans by 40% by year-end. Johnson said higher interest rates will have the greatest impact on some of the REIT's pre-2023 investments, which is why it's prioritizing the sale of older loans. Blackstone Mortgage Trust's total net revenue rose to $141.9M from $132.6M in the same period in 2025 , but interest and related income fell to $280.6M from approximately $346M a year ago, below the Visible Alpha consensus of $293.5M, according to Seeking Alpha . items.title: 'Distress Is Finally Trading': Investors Chasing Big Discounts On Boston Office
items.description: For years following the pandemic, the uncertainty around the office sector left some of the most prominent towers in Boston stuck in limbo and unable to sell to investors that could give them new life. But now, owners and lenders are ready to move on from buildings, even at substantial discounts, and they are being scooped up by buyers who say the price is finally right. Google Maps Synergy's 265 Franklin St. in downtown Boston "Owners and lenders are starting to really understand that their assets may be great assets but have a broken capital stack," Beacon Capital Partners Managing Director Meredith Majoch said this month at Bisnow ’s Boston State of the Market event. "We're starting to see some real liquidity at that end of the market." Majoch said the bidding pool for these types of assets has gotten more competitive. Her firm has sought these opportunities and has lost out on several bids for office properties, but ultimately, she thinks the sales are good for the market. "Distress is finally trading, which is wonderful to see," she said. Majoch was one of several office market players at Bisnow ’s event who discussed the appeal of buying these buildings at such a low cost basis. While many institutional players remain on the sidelines — firms like life insurance companies and pension funds that want steady, predictable returns — opportunistic private investors and foreign buyers see these prices as a prime opportunity to buy low in a city they believe will succeed over the long term. "If we were playing a drinking game where you hear ‘basis’ and drink, we'd all be drunk by now. But it's truly what's going on right now in Boston," North Colony Asset Management partner Drew Pepoli said. "Our investors are pounding down the door, saying, 'Let's buy more. Let's buy more.'" In the third quarter, $2.2B worth of Boston office buildings sold, a 23.7% year-over-year increase, according to Avison Young . Some of these buildings have been trading at well below their past sale prices. Bisnow/Jon Banister Boston Realty Advisors' Jason Weissman and North Colony Asset Management's Drew Pepoli In June, Kendall Capital acquired an 11-story office building at 18 Tremont St. for $30M . The seller, Jamestown , had bought the building in 2019 for $103M. In July, Synergy and New York-based alternative investment manager Axonic Capital acquired the 360K SF building at 265 Franklin St. for $116M from Clarendon Group — 32% less than the $170M Clarendon paid roughly 20 years ago. This week, Rockpoint bought back its 1.1M SF office building at 100 Summer St. at a foreclosure auction, paying $260M , well below the $806M it initially bought the building for in 2019. Young Park , the CEO of Berkeley Garbe, a joint venture formed this year by German real estate firm Garbe and Berkeley Investments, said he is seeing these discounts becoming more common. As lenders are no longer willing to extend loans in hopes an underperforming asset can be turned around, more properties are coming to the market. "I'm encouraged because I see some opportunities. I even hear that some lenders are giving up on the pretend-and-extend and are kind of taking things to a more logical conclusion," Park said. More opportunity is set to come down the pipeline as billions of dollars worth of loans come due. Bisnow/Jon Banister Bernkopf Goodman's April DaSuta, Berkeley Garbe's Young Park and Cambridge Savings Bank's Ian Brandon From this month through the end of next year, $78B of CMBS loans are reaching their hard maturity, meaning borrowers have no extension options remaining, according to Trepp . The office sector has the most CMBS hard maturities next year, at $7.7B. Cambridge Savings Bank Executive Vice President Ian Brandon said next year's wave of loan maturities will "present a great deal of opportunity." "I'm going to feel some pain as a result," the lender said. "But I think it's something that, in many ways, is going to be a good thing in the long term for the markets." Of the buyers hunting deals now, there has been a lot of demand from foreign investors. These buyers accounted for 17% of the year-to-date investment volume among top U.S. markets, according to Avison Young. "We're seeing the biggest demand is definitely from the international market," Pepoli said. "I mean, the majority of our equity is coming into the U.S., and it's because they're taking that higher-altitude look." Pepoli said these international investors are more willing to bet on Boston because they are looking at the long-term fundamentals and aren't as focused on the near-term political issues that might keep other investors away. He said he is also seeing more "smaller shops" like his going after distressed or semidistressed deals right now. North Colony Asset Management has acquired at least three office buildings over the last year, including a 251K SF office building at 10-20 Channel Center St. in January for $52M. The deal is substantially less than the $119M LaSalle Investment Management bought it for in 2016. Pepoli said the real recovery will occur when institutional investors become more willing to buy older office buildings that have been repositioned — helping drive up prices and creating profits for the smaller players investing in upgrades. While institutions are now willing to buy top-tier office buildings like One Marina Park Drive , which Oxford Properties paid $435M for in August, he said they still haven’t been active in the Class-B segment. "Until the institutions start getting their feet wet again in there, there isn't really a huge exit market for when you've executed on these business plans," he said. items.title: Shadow loan fraud: The post-close risk servicers can't see
items.description: Shadow loan fraud: The post-close risk servicers can't see By Brad Finkelstein CloseText About Brad twitter nmnbrad mailto bradley.finkelstein@arizent.com linkedin brad-finkelstein-8b2b9a5/ Published October 29, 2026, 4:59 p.m. EDT 9 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email When a title insurance policy is obtained by the lender or borrower, the items which are covered are only until the time of the search. Processing Content But many deceptions involving title affect ownership of the property, including what Default Analytics describes as shadow loan fraud; these occur after the loan closes and also out of the view of the servicer . What shadow loan fraud is This form of deceit takes place "outside of the main vision of the people that are looking for it," said John Boyd, the founding principal of Default Analytics. John Boyd is the founding principal of Default Analytics It is the kind of deception that isn't seen by the originator through to the investor, he said, adding "It's really a danger that they're not even aware that lurks out there, kind of lurking in the shadows." In a normal property transaction, the buyer acquires the property with a note along with a mortgage or a deed of trust , creating the financial obligation. Most mortgage contracts have a due-on-sale clause; this can apply for other reasons as well, including the transfer of the title, Boyd said. "What happens is the property owner transfers the deed, but doesn't bother to satisfy the corresponding note and mortgage, either with the lender's consent or without," Boyd said. An assumption of the mortgage can be a "sub two," or "subject to," transaction, he said, meaning the buyer takes title while the seller's existing loan stays in place. "But an assumption is done on the premise that the lender has knowledge. A sub two is specifically structured that way, so that the lender does not have knowledge and is not directly notified of that transfer." Bill Corbet, managing director of Blackfin Group's strategic consulting practice (Blackfin has a business relationship with Default Analytics), added the servicing ecosystem works on the premise the borrower and the property owner are one and the same, and have the same interests. Those could diverge with shadow loan fraud. Why it is spreading? Today, social media posters, particularly on YouTube, are "aggressively promoting how to acquire properties without engaging the existing lender," Corbet said. Viewers are asking if such tactics are legal and the posters tend to skirt around actually answering the question, he continued. "That's something very different than what we've seen before in the industry," Corbet said. "There are always creative bad actors out there, but now with social media, their ideas are getting spread literally to hundreds of thousands of people." "Where we find ourselves now is with a lot of — we'll call it — nefarious activity going on, where individuals are coaching persons on how to acquire properties in creative ways," said industry compliance attorney John Levonick , who is also a member of the Default Analytics board of directors. Social media is helping spread the word. People are learning how to convert an owner-occupied mortgage to an investment property, the title is transferred to a business and the noteholder is not aware of the change. Why the industry has looked away Sub two fraud historically has been "somewhat ignored," Boyd said, with the attitude being as long as the payments are being made, no one is being hurt. "The movement of title has been an issue that the industry has dealt with over the years," Levonick said. But in situations where the loan continues to get paid off after the title transfer, the industry has historically turned a blind eye because in a lot of cases it is an innocuous situation and the response has been "no big harm, no big foul," he said. It typically happens when the property is placed in a living trust. Boyd noted some sub two transactions have legit motivations behind them and everything works out fine and all parties benefit. But when things go wrong, it becomes problematic. "That's not the case," he said. "It damages the whole ecosystem when these transactions transpire." For most lenders, title is the thing they look least at because they trust that the title insurer and the policy will take care of the situation if something like an unrecorded lien is found. "I'm not disparaging title companies, I think they do a really important job," said Suzy Lindblom, managing director, national operations and credit at Acra Lending, who is also a member of the Default Analytics advisory council. But I do think it's a lender's responsibility to look at that title, and I honestly think that is the least that people look at." What it costs servicers and lenders The ultimate ding for the servicer is having to write the entire loan off because of this fraud. For seller/servicers, Levonick pointed out that "an innocuous change" in who is on the title can trigger an investor repurchase demand under standard contractual terms. A concern for servicers is these non-monetary ownership changes are also inflating the property's valuation, Lindblom said. Many of these transfers are using a limited liability company to also obfuscate the ownership. "It's transferred from one LLC to another, and these LLCs typically have the same partners," Lindblom said. "Most lenders, when they lend to an LLC, anybody that has 25% or more ownership in that LLC has [provided a] personal guarantee," Lindblom said. "So you see these percentages change by LLC, but they could all be owned by the same people." Having LLC investors makes it easier for the fraudsters to hide, because those looking for it are not seeing common names, but rather anonymous entities, she said. items.title: Biggest US homebuilder misses estimates, sees fewer closings
items.description: Biggest US homebuilder misses estimates, sees fewer closings By Dina Katgara Published October 29, 2026, 4:12 p.m. EDT 1 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email D.R. Horton Inc., the biggest US homebuilder, reported earnings that missed analyst estimates and said it expects to keep offering more discounts than usual to entice sluggish buyers. Processing Content The company reported earnings per share of $2.67 in the fourth quarter, below the average analyst estimate of $3.02 compiled by Bloomberg. D.R. Horton now expects to close fewer home sales in the coming fiscal year, forecasting as few as 79,000 closings in 2027 compared to about 84,000 this year. Rising rates, affordability constraints and cautious consumer sentiment pressured demand in the quarter, Executive Chairman David Auld said in a statement. READ MORE: DR Horton fights RICO suit over lowballed escrow estimates "There's just a lot of noise today out there," Chief Executive Officer Paul Romanowski said in a call with analysts Thursday. "It would be nice to go through a spring without an additional shock or something coming out there so that people can settle down" and buy homes, he said. D.R. Horton focuses on entry-level buyers sensitive to borrowing cost changes. items.title: Zillow OKs $212 million settlement in suit over iBuying failure
items.description: Zillow OKs $212 million settlement in suit over iBuying failure By Andrew Martinez CloseText About Andrew twitter andrewomartinez mailto andrew.martinez@arizent.com linkedin andrewomartinez Published October 29, 2026, 3:47 p.m. EDT 3 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: See why Zillow agreed to a $212.5 million settlement over its defunct homebuying program. Supporting Data: By the third quarter of 2021, the iBuying unit had to sell off 7,000 homes, and cost Zillow hundreds of millions of dollars in writedowns. Zillow is paying a whopping settlement to get rid of a class action lawsuit over the demise of its massive iBuyer program earlier this decade. The real estate giant said Wednesday it agreed to a $212.5 million deal to resolve a longstanding class action lawsuit accusing the firm of misleading investors about the performance of Zillow Offers . The settlement is one of the largest payouts in the industry in recent years , and is a costly coda for a homebuying initiative that collapsed during the refinance boom. Processing Content The Zillow Offers program was created in 2018, and was responsible for up to 70% of purchase leads for the company's Zillow Home Loans origination arm. The company in 2021 ramped up its homebuying efforts in a bid to capture market share, but ended up overpaying for thousands of homes in a major misstep. Plaintiffs sued Zillow and its executive leadership for allegedly making false and misleading statements about the unit's performance throughout 2021, despite the company's scrambling behind the scenes. Executives eventually blamed the company's pricing algorithm it had previously touted. In reaching the settlement, Zillow denied wrongdoing. A spokesperson for the company said Zillow was pleased to reach a resolution, while attorneys for plaintiffs didn't respond to requests for comment Thursday. The number of class members, nor attorney's awards, weren't disclosed this week. Why Zillow Offers failed The program helped power Zillow's origination machine to over $1 billion in origination volume by the third quarter of 2021. During that time, the company embarked on a fated effort to catch up to iBuyer rival Opendoor and ramped up its home purchases, offering prices above what its algorithms suggested, the suit said. Whereas the company bought 1,856 homes in the first quarter of 2021, it rapidly increased those purchases to 9,680 in the third quarter alone. At the same time, Zillow also decreased the scope of its home renovations and the prices it paid to contractors, hoping to present sellers with higher financial offers and save costs. Employees began to raise red flags about the home purchasing activity, according to the lawsuit and other media reports, and contractors began to decline work on the Zillow homes. The unit lost Zillow more than $380 million in the third quarter. By November 2021, Zillow was looking to sell off 7,000 homes, and reported massive nine-figure inventory writedowns in the second half of 2021. Zillow closed the Offers program in November 2021, blaming its pricing algorithms, labor issues, and its renovation backlog. Next steps Of the settlement amount, $48 million will be covered by insurance, Zillow noted in a Securities and Exchange Commission filing. The class includes all persons who bought Zillow Class A or Class C stock between Aug. 5, 2021 and Nov. 2, 2021. Both of those stocks lost approximately 41% of their value during that stretch, with the Class A stock falling from a high of $112.50 per share to $65.86 per share by Nov. 3. The Seattle-based business faces a few other class action lawsuits, including a case alleging the firm steered borrowers to its originations arm. The company has denied those accusations. Zillow Home Loans meanwhile has chugged along, posting larger revenue and origination gains in its most recent period. For the second quarter, Zillow reported $84 million in mortgage segment revenue and $2.2 billion in purchase loan volume, both up significantly quarterly and annually. items.description: Freddie Mac's loan acquisitions top Fannie's as rates rise By Bonnie Sinnock CloseText About Bonnie twitter bcynic mailto bonnie.sinnock@arizent.com linkedin bonnie-sinnock-115a829 Published October 29, 2026, 3:27 p.m. EDT 4 Min Read Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Key Insight: See why Freddie Mac's new loan acquisitions moved ahead of Fannie Mae's in the third quarter. What's at Stake: Competition between Fannie and Freddie could make them more willing to open up the credit box for lenders who sell loans to them. A profitable Freddie Mac regained its lead over larger competitor Fannie Mae in single-family loan acquisitions during the third quarter as higher rates intensified competition between them. Freddie, which is the smaller of the two government-sponsored enterprises when it comes to its outstanding portfolio size, reported Thursday that it acquired $98 billion in home mortgages during the fiscal period. Fannie Mae , in comparison, purchased $88 billion in single-family loans. Processing Content These and other numbers in their recent earnings raises the question of what Freddie is doing to capture more loan acquisitions and whether it's opening up the credit box to do it. The latest underwriting indicators in earnings show Freddie's credit score and loan-to-value ratio tolerances are slightly higher, but the growth in credit reserves and some elevated delinquency measures at both GSEs suggests both will be cautious about the size of their credit boxes. "We are growing our financial strength, applying disciplined decision-making and risk management, and continuing to invest in the capabilities that can make the housing system work better," Freddie Mac Chief Financial Officer Jim Whitlinger said in the GSE's earnings call. What underwriting indicators show Whitlinger reported that Freddie's weighted average current loan-to-value ratio was 54% and the equivalent credit score was 755 in the company's third-quarter earnings call. Fannie's equivalent credit score number was 753 and its mark-to-market loan-to-value ratio was 51%. Current or mark-to-market LTVs on the outstanding portfolios account for property value changes and paydowns on loans over time. Weighted averages for original LTVs are generally higher and have averaged more around 78%, according to Fannie. The underwriting metrics for new acquisitions are a subset of the broader portfolio numbers. Whitlinger and others have indicated there may be more caution in that part of the market because slight increases in certain delinquency buckets have been driven by newer vintages. "The year-over-year increase was primarily driven by higher serious delinquency rates for loans originated during 2022 through 2024," Whitlinger said during the call. Both Fannie and Freddie have seen some delinquencies inch up in both their single- and multifamily book, calling for broader risk management. With risk growing, Freddie had to manage a larger-than anticipated shift from a $900 million benefit for credit losses to a $800 million reserve during the quarter, analysts at BTIG noted. Fannie also recorded a shift from a benefit for credit losses to a reserve in the period. All this suggests that for the time being, Freddie and Fannie are keeping an eye on credit, which may limit how much leeway in underwriting they want to use to compete. But they still want to offer some additional support to help consumers afford homes to the extent their delinquency rates and overall financials allow. While some types of arrears are rising, the single-family serious delinquency rate is still historically low at less than 1% at both GSEs. "Financial strength matters because of what it enables us to do," Whitlinger said. "It gives us greater capacity to provide liquidity throughout the economic cycle, support sustainable homeownership and help make housing finance more efficient and affordable." Examples include a lender option that both GSEs now offer to use the modernized VantageScore 4.0 credit metric for loan pricing, which some mortgage companies have said helped them get certain borrowers approved. This was used for 6% of the loans Fredddie bought in the third quarter, Whitlinger said. Other key financial metrics to watch The GSEs so far have shown that they are financially strong from a net income perspective and have sustained the long run of profitability that followed their 2008 move into conservatorship. So long as that financial strength persists, they might do more to expand some underwriting selectively with offsetting, more conservative adjustments in other areas in line with the trend seen in the condo market. Freddie reported that quarterly net income rose by around 17% on the year to $3.2 billion, and Fannie announced a day earlier that its strongest net revenues since 2023 drove an 8% increase during the same period to $4.2 billion. The smaller GSE's $3.2 billion in growth for the quarter also brought its total net worth to $81 billion, helping to close a regulatory capital gap that's also essential to their financial soundness and an eventual conservatorship exit. Fannie also reported improvement in this area. "Excluding buffers, our capital shortfall was $98 billion at the end of third quarter 2026, largely because the $73 billion of senior preferred stock does not qualify," Whitlinger said in a reminder that an exit would need to address this, a key point prominent GSE investors have emphasized. items.title: Los Angeles Rental Report 2026Q3: Renters Catch a Break as New Supply Pushes Rents Lower; Buying Still Costs Nearly $5,000 More a Month
items.description: Los Angeles Rental Report 2026Q3: Renters Catch a Break as New Supply Pushes Rents Lower; Buying Still Costs Nearly $5,000 More a Month By Jiayi Xu , Danielle Hale Oct 29, 2026 Highlights In 2026Q3, the median asking rent in Los Angeles County registered at $2,554,—down $96, or 3.6%, from a year earlier. The median asking rent for 0-2 bedrooms in L.A. County was $2,239, reflecting a decline of $88 (-3.8%) from the previous year. Meanwhile, rent for 3+ bedroom units dropped by $70 (-1.9%) compared to 2025Q3, standing at $3,571. For renters in L.A. County : Buying costs far more than renting. In 2026Q3, a median-priced home cost $4,716 more a month than renting one, nearly 185% higher, even though the monthly buying cost fell about 2% as home prices dropped. Mortgage rates above 7% could erase that relief. At 7%, the same home would cost about $7,456 a month, roughly where it stood a year ago, erasing the savings from lower prices In the third quarter of 2026, the median asking rent for all rental properties listed on Realtor.com in Los Angeles County was $2,554, a decline of $96, or 3.6%, compared with a year ago. While the county experienced a temporary dip in rents during the pandemic, asking rents quickly rebounded to pre-pandemic levels and peaked in the summer of 2022. Since then, a surge in new multifamily construction has put sustained downward pressure on rent. In the most recent quarter, the median asking rent in Los Angeles County was $340, or 11.7%, below its 2022 peak. In addition, Los Angeles County renters are overwhelmingly local. In the third quarter of 2026, more than half (61.3%) of online traffic to L.A. County rental listings originated from within the county, with an additional 15.5% coming from elsewhere in California. Out-of-state renters accounted for 19.8% of traffic, while international traffic represented 3.4%. Breaking down by bedroom type, the median asking rent for 0-2 bedroom units in Los Angeles County was $2,239 in 2026Q3, a decline of $88 or 3.8%, from a year ago. Larger units with three or more bedrooms saw a comparatively modest softening, with a median asking rent of $3,571 — down $70, or 1.9%, year-over-year. The steeper rent decline among smaller units suggests renters in that segment are experiencing greater pricing relief. The surge in ADUs across Los Angeles County may partially explain this trend. As those permitted units complete construction — typically requiring 6 to 18 months from permit to occupancy — a growing wave of new small rental units has been entering the market, adding downward price pressure concentrated in the smaller unit segment. County Rents by Unit Size, 2026Q3 Unit Size Median Asking Rent Rent YoY vs. Peak Overall $2,554 -3.6% -11.7% 0-2 beds $2,239 -3.8% -14.7% 3+ beds $3,571 -1.9% -11.3% City of Los Angeles: Relief from the peak, but still out of reach for many In the third quarter of 2026, the median asking rent for rental properties listed on Realtor.com in the City of Los Angeles was $2,708, reflecting a decline of $92, or 3.3%, from a year earlier. Consistent with the broader L.A. County trend, rents in the City of Los Angeles have been on a downward trajectory since peaking in the summer of 2022. While the current median remains $158, or 5.5%, above pre-pandemic levels, renters today are saving $363 per month, or 11.8%, compared to the 2022 peak, translating to $4,356 in annual savings. Nevertheless, in order to afford a typical home in the city of Los Angeles, a minimum annual income of $108,320 is required— 22.1% higher than the city's estimated median household income of $88,730 1 High mortgage rates squeeze renters hoping to buy Renters may be catching a break, but for most renters who want to become homeowners in L.A. County, homeownership remains out of reach. On top of that, with mortgage rates now above 7%, higher borrowing costs could push homeownership even further out of reach for renters who want to buy. In 2026Q3, buying a typical home in L.A. County costs $4,716 more per month than renting one. Buying got slightly cheaper over the past year because home prices fell, even as mortgage rates rose. The median listing price dropped 3.2% to $970,000 over the past year, which more than offset a small increase in the average 30-year fixed mortgage rate, from 6.57% to 6.68%. As a result, the estimated monthly cost of buying a median-priced home fell about 2.1%, or $159, from a year earlier, to $7,270. But that relief may not last. Rates surpassed 7% in late-September and remain well- above this mark. At 7%, the same home price would cost about $7,456 a month, roughly where it stood a year ago, erasing the monthly payment savings from lower prices. Methodology To determine the monthly cost of buying a home, we find the median listing price for homes in Los Angeles County. As first-time homebuyers plan lower down payments, we assume a 10% down payment and use the 30-year fixed mortgage rate during the quarter to calculate a monthly mortgage payment. We also include the HOA fees, taxes, and homeowners insurance as part of the costs. L.A. rental data as of 2026Q3 for all units advertised for rent on Realtor.com®. Rental units include apartments as well as private rentals (condos, townhomes, single-family homes). We use rental sources that reliably report data each month within L.A. county. To calculate the median asking rent for each quarter, we first obtain the median asking rent for each month within that quarter and then take the average of the three months. items.title: Luxury Cut: The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking
items.description: Luxury Cut: The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking By Anthony Smith Oct 29, 2026 The Fall 2026 Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking St Louis Downtown and Arch – SeanPavonePhoto/Adobe Stock St. Louis Returns to the Top St. Louis has made its way back to the top spot this quarter in the Wall Street Journal/Realtor.com Luxury Housing Market Ranking. The top 5 rounds out with Charlottesville, VA; Portland, ME; Bridgeport, CT; and Pittsfield, MA, which took the top spot last quarter. Common themes across the top-ranked markets include low climate risk, lower unemployment rates, and higher levels of buyer demand. Each quarter, Realtor.com and the Wall Street Journal team up to identify the highest-performing and most attractive metro areas for luxury home purchases. We score 60 different luxury housing markets across the country in categories that include supply and demand strength, economic health, and quality of life. This fall’s ranking points to a return to fundamentals: markets with active buyer demand, homes that sell at a steady pace, and low exposure to climate risk moved to the front of the pack, while several lifestyle-driven markets that led earlier this year slipped out of the top 10. Highlights St. Louis climbs from No. 12 to No. 1 , reclaiming the top spot it last held in summer 2025, backed by the lowest cost of living in the ranking, strong buyer demand, and minimal climate risk. Four new entries joined the top 10 : St. Louis, Portland, ME (No. 3), Bridgeport, CT (No. 4), and Detroit (No. 6). Charlottesville, VA, reaches No. 2 , its highest placement yet, extending its run to six straight quarters in the top 10. Four markets exited the top 10 . Boulder, CO, fell from No. 2 to No. 15. San Jose, CA, dropped from No. 3 to No. 37. Santa Fe, NM, slipped from No. 4 to No. 16, and Santa Barbara, CA, moved from No. 10 to No. 17. St. Louis last topped the list in summer 2025 and held the No. 2 spot last fall and at the beginning of this year. Beyond the lower cost of living, the metro also has strong demand and low climate risk.
