items.title: Beloved ‘Star Trek’ Actor Patrick Stewart Dies at Home in Los Angeles
items.description: Actor Patrick Stewart , celebrated for his legendary roles in "Star Trek: The Next Generation" and all five "X-Men" movies, died in his Los Angeles, CA home on Wednesday, Oct. 28 at the age of 86. "We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer's Disease and Lewy Body Dementia," an Oct. 29 Instagram post shared to Stewart's account reads. "He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayers, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all," the statement continued. "We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace." A Yorkshire, England native, Stewart split his time between his homes in California , Park Slope, Brooklyn , and the United Kingdom. In a 2014 discussion with Vanity Fair , he explained that he had always dreamt of moving to the United States, having seen aspirational American homes on screen. Loading... Legendary "Star Trek" actor Patrick Stewart has passed away in his Los Angeles home at the age of 86. Aaron Rapoport/Corbis/Getty Images Loading... The Yorkshire native split his time between his homes in California, New York, and the United Kingdom. Paul Harris/Getty Images "The movies were my passion when I was a child," he explained, noting that he didn't own a television until he was 26 years old. "I loved movies about American life. I was growing up in a working-class neighborhood in a very small house, and I loved movies about American homes with green lawns and beautiful, big kitchens, and so it was the glamour of American life as it was portrayed in the movies." Eventually, it was a film called "On the Waterfront" that introduced Stewart to Red Hook, Brooklyn, a location he'd later live just "a block away from." "I saw that movies could be about something other than pure escapism and fantasy," he said, noting that the film was "actually about the kind of people" that he was used to spending time around as a child. Brooklyn was also the place where Stewart met his wife, Sunny Ozell , 47, in 2008. "She was working as a waitress in a restaurant in Brooklyn," Stewart told People magazine of the chance encounter. "This lovely woman came over and said, 'Gentlemen, on the house, what would you like for desserts?'" As the pair got to talking, Stewart—who was starring in a Brooklyn Academy of Music production of "Macbeth" at the time—learned Ozell had been hoping to see the show, but was disappointed that the limited run had been sold out before opening. He gave Ozell his phone number, and promised to secure her a ticket. "And that's what we did," he shared. "And she came backstage afterward and we had dinner and here we are." The couple married in 2013, residing in a Park Slope duplex penthouse the actor purchased for $2.5 million the year prior, according to Business Insider. The 2,176-square-foot home boasted 11-foot ceilings and a converted carriage house. A year later, Stewart explained that he and Ozell had fully embraced a Brooklyn lifestyle—jokingly citing the amount of kale that they ate at the time, and quipping that he was planning on "beginning a campaign" to ban "strollers from sidewalks." In the same interview, Stewart revealed he was planning to spend "a large part of the summer" in his home in "a very pretty part of the U.K." Although Stewart would later offload the idyllic Yorkshire Dales home he was referring to in 2016, the decision to reside in two countries was an intentional move to stay connected to his roots. "I was fearful of losing myself to Hollywood in the way I'd seen other British stage actors do," he told The Yorkshire Post after selling his home. "I wanted a toehold in England, somewhere to come home to." In 2019, Stewart purchased the former home of "Modern Family" director Jason Winer—a 4,500-square-foot Los Angeles estate he snapped up for $4.3 million, according to Yahoo! Finance . items.title: Passengers Who Sold Their Homes for a $120K ‘Perpetual Cruise’ Are Now Stranded in Cambodia
items.description: Randy Cassingham thought he was embarking on the adventure of a lifetime—a never-ending cruise that would take him around the world and across multiple continents. That was the promise of Villa Vie Residences’ Odyssey cruise, set to visit 147 countries and 425 ports over a period of 3.5 years. Passengers had three options: They could rent a villa through the Odyssey’s “rent-to-own” program starting at $3,499 a month, which allowed passengers to join the cruise at any point along the way. Or they could purchase a five-year residency on the cruise ship starting at $59,999. The final option was a permanent residency—good for the life of the cruise ship—which started at $119,999, with villa suites going for as much as $439,999. Villa Vie is still advertising these cabins as available on its website. Cassingham was among many passengers who sold their belongings—including their homes—for the chance to live aboard a cruise ship for the rest of his life. “We were planning on being on for, you know, forever,” Cassingham told the Times Radio . “They were guaranteeing that this ship would last 15 years and I think it was in good enough shape that it could have. And that was our plan. We were going to stay there until we decided we didn't want to do it anymore or we died. One or the other.” But just two years on, Cassingham’s “never-ending cruise” came to an abrupt end. Earlier this week, Villa Vie told the 200 or so passengers aboard the Odyssey that they would have to disembark in Cambodia because the company could no longer afford to run the ship. Villa Vie said the culprit was the rising cost of fuel due to the war in Iran and repeated closures of the Strait of Hormuz. According to Villa Vie’s estimates, per-cabin fuel expenses rose from $1,800 to between $6,000 and $8,000 per month, putting “its current operating model under unsustainable financial pressure.” “Since the conflict [in Iran] began in late February, we have taken significant steps to reduce fuel consumption, including slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port,” the company’s statement continued. “Those measures have not been enough to offset the extraordinary increase in fuel costs, and we have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses.” It also probably didn't help that the 650-capacity ship was never fully booked. Villa Vie said on its website that the Odyssey was 85% sold, but Cassingham said he believed that the ship topped out at around 350 passengers. Residents said they had been aware of ongoing financial issues. Pamela Reckamp told NBC News that at a September meeting, ship officials asked residents to help raise $1 million so they could refuel the ship in Vietnam. Loading... A passenger walks through the empty Odyssey cruise ship after travelers on the ship were asked to disembark in Cambodia because the ship ran out of fuel. TANG CHHIN Sothy / AFP via Getty Images On Monday morning, passengers heard an announcement coming over the loudspeaker: “Unfortunately, they were unable to secure the fuel necessary to continue operations. As a result, the Odyssey will officially enter a ‘temporary layup’ this afternoon. All residents must disembark by 2 p.m. today.” In a press release, Villa Vie said it would be “working to support those affected as plans develop.” However, a blog post on Cassingham’s website, Residential Cruising , contradicted that. “The company has done absolutely nothing to help,” he wrote. “We couldn’t even walk out of the port, so there were shuttle buses that dropped us in the middle of town, Sihanoukville, Cambodia, the end. They didn’t even give us a list of hotels, let alone help us get there or pay for them.” That left Cassingham and many other passengers bewildered about what to do next. “We had built a house, and it was our dream house, and we decided to sell that and our cars and almost all of our belongings and move onto the ship full-time permanently,” he told Radio Times. “We don't have a home to go to right now. We don't know what we're going to do exactly.” Realtor.com® has reached out to Villa Vie Residences for comment. Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. items.title: Invitation Homes Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results
items.description:
Earnings Press Release
Invitation Homes Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results
Dallas, TX, October 28, 2026 — Invitation Homes Inc. (NYSE: INVH) (“Invitation Homes,” “we,” “our,” and “us”), the nation’s
premier single-family home leasing and management company, today announced our Third Quarter (“Q3”) 2026 financial and
operating results.


Q3 2026 Highlights
•   Year over year, total revenues increased 6.3% to $731 million, property operating and maintenance costs increased 2.0% to
    $264 million, and net income available to common stockholders increased 15.6% to $158 million, or $0.27 per diluted
    common share.
•   Year over year, Core FFO per share increased 2.4% to $0.48, while AFFO per share increased 0.1% to $0.38.
•   Same Store NOI increased 1.1% year over year on 1.6% Same Store Core Revenues growth and 2.5% Same Store Core
    Operating Expenses growth.
•   Same Store Average Occupancy was 96.4%, a reduction of 10 basis points year over year.
•   Same Store renewal rent growth of 4.3% and Same Store new lease rent growth of (0.2)% resulted in Same Store blended
    rent growth of 3.0%.
•   We sold 658 wholly owned homes, most to families purchasing for their own use, and acquired 216 wholly owned homes,
    for net dispositions of 442 homes and net proceeds of approximately $245 million that we used to fund share repurchases.
•   As previously announced, on July 8, 2026, we closed a public offering of $500 million aggregate principal amount of 4.950%
    senior notes (the “Notes”). The Notes were priced at 99.291% of the principal amount and mature on February 1, 2032. Net
    proceeds were used to prepay a portion of our secured debt obligation maturing in June 2027.


Capital Allocation Update
From December 1, 2025 through October 27, 2026, we bought back nearly $1 billion of our shares. This includes an aggregate
of 36,923,753 shares repurchased to date at an average stock price of $26.78, and represents an implied value per home of
approximately $280,000 against a gross average sales price of approximately $460,000 for homes sold during that same period.


On October 26, 2026, our board of directors authorized an additional $500 million share repurchase program.


Comments from Chief Executive Officer Dallas Tanner
“Our third quarter reflected steady execution across the platform. Same Store NOI grew 1.1% year over year, blended rent growth
was 3.0%, and with the benefit of our share repurchases, Core FFO per share grew 2.4%. Since December 2025, we’ve
repurchased nearly $1 billion of our stock at a substantial valuation discount. We believe that is more than any other residential
REIT. With the new $500 million share repurchase program our board just authorized, we intend to keep funding buybacks with
home sale proceeds whenever our stock trades at a meaningful discount to the value of our homes, guided by market conditions
and a disciplined approach to the balance sheet.”


“Following a solid third quarter, we are raising our full year guidance midpoints for Core FFO per share by $0.01 to $1.96, Same
Store NOI growth guidance to 1.2%, and wholly owned home sales to $950 million, which supports our continued focus on
closing the gap between public and private market values.”
 Glossary & Reconciliations of Non-GAAP Financial and Other Operating Measures
Financial and operating measures found in the Earnings Release and Supplemental Information include certain measures used by
Invitation Homes management that are measures not defined under accounting principles generally accepted in the United States
(“GAAP”). These measures are defined herein and, as applicable, reconciled to the most comparable GAAP measures.

items.title: Mortgage Rates
items.description: Mortgage Rates Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® (PMMS ® ) results are based on the mortgage rate collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac through Loan Product Advisor ® (LPA ® ) from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. Learn more in our FAQs . Primary Mortgage Market Survey ® U.S. weekly mortgage rate averages as of 10/29/2026 30-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 7.24% 15-year Fixed-Rate Mortgage 6.60% Download Rates Since 1971 Mortgage Rates Decline Further to 7.24% The average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage declined again this week, reaching its lowest level this month and modestly boosting purchasing power for prospective buyers. The 30-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 7.24% as of October 29, 2026, down from last week when it averaged 7.32%. A year ago at this time, the 30-year FRM averaged 6.17%. The 15-year fixed-rate mortgage averaged 6.60%, down from last week when it averaged 6.68%. A year ago at this time, the 15-year FRM averaged 5.41%. PMMS results are released weekly on Thursdays at 12 p.m. ET. and are an average of loan rates offered the prior Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Compare Historical PMMS Results Frequently Asked Questions Toggle all accordion sections Expand All What data is used for PMMS? The PMMS results are based on data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA): mortgage rates collected from thousands of loan applications submitted to Freddie Mac from lenders across the country when a borrower applies for a mortgage. For more detailed information, see Enhanced Mortgage Rate Survey Explained . How is the national average determined? We collect the mortgage rate of all purchase applications based on PMMS criteria and a national average mortgage rate is calculated out of all the selected loan applications. The criteria include weekly conventional, single-family originations with conforming loan limits as set by FHFA. Is the PMMS rate based on current lender quotes or recent settlements? PMMS rates are based on applications submitted to Freddie Mac for the given week from lenders across the country. What type of lenders are included in the PMMS? Currently, our lenders are a mix of credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies. Do the PMMS results represent the rates charged on a specific day of the week? If so, which day? Or are they the average rate charged that week? PMMS is published each Thursday at noon ET. When a U.S. holiday falls on a Thursday, the PMMS will publish on the Wednesday of that week. The week of application activity starts at 12:00 a.m. ET the prior Thursday and lasts through 11:59 p.m. ET Wednesday. Therefore, the PMMS results are an average of loan rates offered Thursday through Wednesday. See our publication calendar . Why are adjustable rates no longer published? ARMs indexed to alternatives to U.S. Treasury securities have become more prevalent in the market. As we worked on enhancing the PMMS , we carefully considered which loan products were most popular for the PMMS borrower profile (good/excellent credit, 20% loans, home purchase loans on owner occupied 1-unit single-family properties). Additionally, in recent years the mortgage market has been dominated by fixed mortgage products. While there has been an uptick recently in the share of adjustable-rate mortgages (ARMs) for the broader mortgage market, ARMs remain most popular for higher loan size (nonconforming) loans. Why are fees/points no longer published? Under the current LPA requirements, fees and points are not always required to be provided by lenders. Therefore, we are not able to report on the average fees and points. How has PMMS changed over time? Since April 1971, Freddie Mac shared the average 30-year fixed-rate mortgage rate with the PMMS. We have updated the information we collect and the process for gathering data over time. Changes in Data Processes When it was launched, PMMS surveyed lenders on the rates and points for their most popular 30-year fixed-rate, 15-year fixed-rate and 5/1 hybrid amortizing adjustable-rate mortgage products. The survey was based on first-lien prime conventional conforming home purchase mortgages with a loan-to-value of 80 percent. In addition, the adjustable-rate mortgage (ARM) products were indexed to U.S. Treasury yields, and lenders were asked for both the initial coupon rate and points as well as the margin on the ARM products. Lenders surveyed each week were a mix of lender types — credit unions, commercial banks and mortgage lending companies — roughly proportional to the level of mortgage business that each type commands nationwide. On November 17, 2022, the mortgage rate gathering process was updated. Instead of surveying lenders, we now use data from our Loan Product Advisor (LPA). items.title: U.S. Retail Demand Remains Solid as Limited Construction Keeps Space Tight
items.description: U.S. Retail Demand Remains Solid as Limited Construction Keeps Space Tight Phoebe Schmidt • 10/29/2026 Q3 U.S. Retail Marketbeat Shopping centers recorded 3.5 million square feet of net absorption in Q3, with fitness, wellness and value retailers leading leasing activity New York -- U.S. shopping center demand remained solid in the third quarter of 2026 as retailers backfilled vacated stores and selectively expanded their footprints, according to Cushman & Wakefield's latest U.S. Retail MarketBeat report . Limited construction continued to support market fundamentals, with national vacancy holding steady at 5.9%, well below the historical average of 7.4%. Net absorption totaled 3.5 million square feet in Q3, the second-strongest quarterly reading since Q4 2023, bringing year-to-date absorption into positive territory at 1.2 million square feet. The improvement followed first-half declines that reflected seasonal weakness and the effects of store closures in 2025. "Retail demand has remained solid beneath the quarterly fluctuations," said James Bohnaker , Principal Economist at Cushman & Wakefield. "Retailers are backfilling space left by earlier closures and continuing to expand selectively. For tenants looking to grow, finding the right space in a quality shopping center remains a challenge." Fitness, wellness and value-oriented retailers are leading categories for leasing activity, reflecting a continued shift toward consumer services and demand for affordable shopping options. Discount retailers accounted for 1,046 store openings year to date, while off-price apparel retailers added 214 locations. New construction remained limited, with just 2.3 million square feet delivered during the quarter. The development pipeline represented only 0.4% of existing inventory. National asking rents reached $25.80 per square foot, up 2.2% year over year, although the pace of growth moderated. "With so little new space being built, even modest expansion can keep availability tight," Bohnaker said. "Consumer spending is holding steady, but retailers remain disciplined about where they open stores. Well-located centers with strong tenant mixes are best positioned to capture that demand." Demand was positive across several regions. The West absorbed 1.4 million square feet and remained the only region to record positive absorption in every quarter of 2026, led in Q3 by Phoenix, the Inland Empire and Orange County. The Northeast recorded 1.2 million square feet of absorption, with vacancy declining in eight of its 11 tracked markets. The Midwest led regional asking rent growth at 3.6% year over year, with Columbus, Cincinnati and St. Louis among the strongest-performing markets nationally. The South accounted for 52% of year-to-date construction completions but maintained the lowest regional vacancy rate at 5.7%. Cushman & Wakefield expects retail fundamentals to remain resilient through year-end, supported by limited new supply and continued tenant demand. Performance will vary by market and property, with location, tenant quality and retailers' value propositions remaining key differentiators. Supply Miami-Dade County’s retail construction pipeline remained steady in the third quarter of 2026, with 1.3 million square feet (msf) underway. Construction commenced on nearly 63,000 square feet (sf) of new retail space during the quarter. Meanwhile, deliveries totaled 78,000 sf, bringing year-to-date (YTD) deliveries to 158,000 sf. This represented a 64.6% year-over-year (YOY) decrease from the 447,000 sf delivered during the same period in 2025. Vacancy increased 10 basis points (bps) quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) to 3.1% and rose by the same amount YOY. Despite the slight increase, Miami-Dade County’s retail market continued to demonstrate tight conditions, with vacancy remaining the lowest among Florida markets, below Fort Lauderdale at 4.2%, Orlando at 3.9% and Tampa at 3.8%. Demand Retail leasing activity across Miami-Dade County totaled more than 441,000 sf in the third quarter of 2026, bringing YTD deal volume to 1.7 msf, down 18.0% YOY. The market recorded negative 81,000 sf of net absorption during the quarter, bringing the YTD total to negative 129,000 sf. Although occupancy losses have persisted in six of the past seven quarters, quarterly performance improved considerably from negative 230,000 sf in the third quarter of 2025. At the submarket level, Kendall and Miami Airport led occupancy gains, recording 97,000 sf and nearly 51,000 sf of positive absorption, respectively. These gains were offset by losses in Coral Gables (negative 41,000 sf) and Northeast Dade (negative 35,000 sf). By property type, malls posted the strongest performance, with occupancy gains of just under 12,000 sf, while general retail recorded the largest decline at negative 62,000 sf. Overall, leasing activity and occupancy trends remained mixed across the county, with gains in select submarkets and property types offset by continued weakness elsewhere. Looking ahead, the construction pipeline may provide additional opportunities for retailers as new space enters the market, although future occupancy gains will depend on demand keeping pace with new supply. Pricing Miami-Dade County’s average retail asking rent reached $50.27 per square foot (psf) in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 1.8% increase YOY. Among the county’s retail submarkets, Miami Beach commanded the highest average asking rent at $97.85 psf, while Miami recorded the lowest at $31.92 psf. Compared YOY, average asking rents increased in 16 submarkets and declined in three. Outlying Miami-Dade County recorded the largest YOY increase, with rents rising 4.1% from $40.97 psf to $42.65 psf. In contrast, Brickell asking rents declined 2.4% YOY to $84.96 psf. Retail Sales Miami-Dade County recorded $619.9 million in retail investment sales during the third quarter of 2026, representing almost 810,000 sf sold. This brought YTD transaction volume to $1.2 billion across 2.0 msf. YTD transaction volume declined 25.5% YOY and was 6.6% below the five-year average. Miami Airport led all submarkets with $265.8 million in sales. Notable transactions included the $72.0 million sale of Airpark Plaza, located at 5715 NW Seventh Street in the Miami Airport submarket. By property type, strip malls recorded the highest average sale price at $815 psf during the quarter. Pricing remained elevated, with Miami averaging $450 psf, well above the U.S. average of $246 psf, underscoring the market’s continued premium positioning. Miami-Dade County’s retail capitalization rates ranged from 4.9% to 7.2%, averaging 5.8%. This was below the national average of 7.4%, indicating that local retail properties continued to trade at lower yields than the national average. items.title: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter
items.description: Home Vacancy and 'Zombie' Rates Tick Down in Fourth Quarter by ATTOM Team | Oct 29, 2026 | Foreclosures , Real Estate News - Recent Articles The national vacancy rate declined to 1.2 percent; Zombie home rate dropped slightly to 3 percent IRVINE, Calif. – October 29, 2026 — ATTOM , the leading provider of property data , AI-powered intelligence , and real estate analytics solutions, the leading provider of property data , AI-powered analytics, and real estate intelligence solutions, today released its latest Vacant Property and Zombie Foreclosure Report showing that 1.2 percent of residential properties in the United States were vacant in the final quarter of the year. That was down from 1.3 percent in the third quarter and in the same quarter last year. The report analyzes publicly recorded real estate data collected by ATTOM — including foreclosure status, equity and owner-occupancy status — matched against monthly updated vacancy data. (See full methodology below). There were 269,195 properties in the foreclosure process in the fourth quarter, out of 105.1 million total properties analyzed. Of those properties in foreclosure, 3 percent, or 8,040 properties, were “zombies,” meaning the owners had abandoned the homes before the conclusion of the foreclosure proceedings. The fourth-quarter zombie rate was down from 3.3 percent in the prior quarter and in the same quarter last year. “The fourth-quarter data showed modest declines in both vacancy and zombie foreclosure rates nationwide,” said Rob Barber, CEO of ATTOM. “While trends vary from state to state, vacant and abandoned homes continue to represent a relatively small share of the nation’s housing stock.” Zombie homes on rise in majority of states The number of zombie properties rose quarter-over-quarter in 29 states. Among states with at least 50 zombie properties in the fourth quarter, the largest quarter-over-quarter increases were in Wisconsin (up 20.9 percent to 52 zombie properties), Maryland (up 19.2 percent to 180 zombie properties), Pennsylvania (up 17.2 percent to 252 zombie properties), Texas (up 15.7 percent to 192 zombie properties), and North Carolina (up 15.2 percent to 129 zombie properties). The states with sufficient data to analyze and that had the largest declines in zombie properties were Arizona (down 34.9 percent to 56 zombie properties), Florida (down 19.6 percent to 2,220 zombie properties), California (down 10.4 percent to 267 zombie properties), South Carolina (down 9.6 percent to 141 zombie properties), and Oklahoma (down 8.9 percent to 82 zombie properties). Vacancy rates below half a percent in much of Northeast The states with the highest overall home vacancy rates in the fourth quarter were Oklahoma (2.4 percent), Kansas (2.3 percent), Alabama (2.1 percent), West Virginia (2.1 percent), and Missouri (2 percent). The lowest vacancy rates were in New Hampshire (0.3 percent), Vermont (0.4 percent), New Jersey (0.4 percent), Connecticut (0.4 percent), and Idaho (0.5 percent). Ten metro areas posted no zombie properties There were 164 metropolitan statistical areas with sufficient data to include in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 100,000 residential properties and at least 50 properties in the foreclosure process. The metro areas with the highest zombie rates were Baltimore, MD (13 percent); Youngstown, OH (13 percent); Akron, OH (11.5 percent); Cedar Rapids, IA (10.7 percent); and Scranton, PA (9.4 percent). Ten of the metro areas had no zombie properties, the largest of which were Bridgeport, CT; El Paso, TX; Little Rock, AR; Fayetteville, AR; and Visalia, CA. Vacancy rates higher among investor-owned properties Institutional investors held 30.6 million homes in the fourth quarter, of which 2.7 percent, or 840,384, were vacant. The states with the highest vacancy rates for investor-owned homes were Indiana (6.5 percent), Alabama (5.8 percent), Oklahoma (5.4 percent), Kansas (5.2 percent), and Louisiana (5.1 percent). The lowest vacancy rates for investor-owned properties were in New Hampshire (0.6 percent), Vermont (0.9 percent), Utah (0.9 percent), Hawaii (1 percent), and New Jersey (1.1 percent). Powering Real Estate Businesses with Property Data and Analytics Solutions For Every Industry Zombie rates high in several Baltimore, Indianapolis zip codes There were 2,585 zip codes with sufficient data to be included in ATTOM’s analysis, meaning they had at least 1,000 residential properties and at least 25 in foreclosure in the fourth quarter. Of those, the highest zombie rates were in 21205 in Baltimore, MD (42.5 percent); 21223 in Baltimore, MD (40 percent); 46201 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); 46218 in Indianapolis, IN (32.3 percent); and 13619 in Carthage, NY (32.1 percent). Conclusion ATTOM’s fourth quarter vacancy and zombie home report found that the national vacancy rate fell slightly from the previous quarter to 1.2 percent. The national zombie home rate also dropped to 3 percent.
